I'm taking a leap here but I'm going to assume that the scenario you have in your head for how this would go down isn't that a man would come up to you and suggest that you have sex with him.  Instead, I think you're picturing something like this: you're on a date with a girl.  She's smart, funny, kind, and beautiful.  You have a great time, and agree to see her again.  Second date is also awesome, so of course you set up a third.  At the start of the third date, she says she has something she needs to tell you before things get too serious.  She's transgender.  

At that point, your entire perception of her is deflated.  You feel lied to and disgusted.  Of course this is the tamer scenario, as opposed to the one where you get all the way to bed with her, have great heterosexual sex, and then you find out.

So, if I'm right, the issue isn't actually that you're not attracted to trans people.  It's that you admit that you could be, and it disgusts you.  THAT is transphobic.  

However, I could be wrong, and you could be envisioning a completely different scenario for how this issue might actually impact your life.  You could be assuming that you'd be able to tell immediately if someone was trans--which is also transphobic because not all trans people look the same.  Or you could be assuming that all trans women have penises--which is also transphobic for the same reason.  

Finally I want to point out that by likening trans people to pedophiles you already crossed the point of no return on any trans person thinking you're not transphobic.

> A blanket rule against having sex with trans women, even "pre-op" trans women, is necessarily transphobic.

Stupidest thing I've heard. That's like saying refusing to have sex with men makes you homophobic.

We structure our concept of sexuality around gender.  "Homosexual," "heterosexual," "pansexual," etc are all rooted in an idea that the first baseline of attraction is gender.  

If someone says they're a heterosexual man, it's implying that they're exclusively attracted to women.  So no one would argue that this identity is prejudiced against men, because it's not singling men out.  Being a heterosexual man who refuses to have sex with men is perfectly in line with our beliefs about sexuality.

But when you remove a specific group of women from your potential sex-ing pool due to their physical characteristics, with no possibility of exception, it's considered prejudicial.  Saying that you'd never have sex with an Asian woman is racist.  Saying that you'd never have sex with a Muslim woman is Islamophobic.  Saying that you'd never have sex with a disabled woman is ableist.  Because you're assuming certain traits about those women and excluding them as a category based on those assumptions.  You're pre-judging them as inherently undesirable, even though they meet the criteria of your stated sexuality.

According to your criteria, saying "I'm not attracted to transwomen" is bigoted, but "I am a cisheterosexual man" would not be.

Also, you say "we" "believe" this about sexuality. Who is we? Why must everyone conform to these theories of sexuality or else have a moral failing?

Hoo boy here we go again.  You cannot know with certainty that someone is or is not trans without them telling you.  You cannot know that your cisheterosexuality is being met or not.

And, I mean, sure, you could personally claim that you just don't conform to these theories of sexuality.  I personally think that delineating one's sexuality by gender is rapidly becoming obsolete, for many of the reasons that I have outlined here.  But seeing as you're still going to label yourself, not to mention date within, that system, it's a pretty futile thing to do.

It doesn't matter if I can't tell the difference visually. A blind person can't either, but they're not all pansexual.

What is your definition of a libertarian? I'll go with Google's definition; an extreme laissez-faire political philosophy advocating only minimal state intervention in the lives of citizens.

I consider myself a cultural (or "speech") libertarian, in that I believe that the government should have no intervention on speech. Politically, I actually lean liberal. I am pro-choice and think that birth control should be a universal right, as an example.

>[they] ignore that political correctness is what has kept many closet racists from coming out of the closet

Political correctness stops speech. That's what it is. Even if they're wrong, they should have the right to say that "women are scientifically unsuitable for some jobs". This lets us counter their argument in public with facts and logic, if we can. But we'll never get to the bottom of it without being allowed to discuss it.

Nobody should be killed by police unless they are an immediate threat to others. The problem is that black people commit a disproportionate amount of crime and thus have a disproportionate amount of interaction with police. This boils down to differences in judgment about what makes something immoral. Vegans living a life of convenience in every other aspect of their life except their diet claiming that eating meat is immoral sounds to me like saying that raping 1 guy is "less immoral" than raping 50 guys. And perhaps you think that, but I don't. I think rape is just morally reprehensible, period.
Eliminating suffering is of course impossible, and by extension, it's silly to assert that the inability to do something which is impossible is immoral. "Reducing suffering" is the more appropriate call, but that's vague and unquantifiable in any reasonable way. How much suffering needs to be reduced before I get a gold morality star? How come you get to pick the way in which I reduce suffering? I mean, maybe this is a pretty good and efficient way of reducing suffering, but just because something is effective does not make it a *moral requirement*. 
Basically, the argument against eating meat is an emotionally charged dogma. There are lots of good reasons to go vegan, but to go so far as to say that it is *immoral not to* is completely untenable without relying massively on an appeal to emotion.

The current generation does seem to be much more concerned with animal welfare than previous ones, so it's not unlikely that future ones will find the way we treat animals pretty alarming. This is not necessarily because it is "immoral" though.

I also do not believe that the welfare of non-humans matters as much as the welfare of humans--it's really hard to defend any ideas about objective morality without an appeal to dogma or emotion, but I believe the implied empathetic contract we have with each other dictates reasonable behavior among humans. And you can not have a "contract" with an unwitting party.
